title: Moving to Chicago at 15: first impressions, jobs and being discovered
summary: She contrasts New Orleans and Chicago, describes laundry and factory work, and being heard at a funeral by a record scout who recorded her religious songs.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

biggest difference between life in New Orleans and life in Chicago well when I the first impression ever made on me when I got off the train in Chicago that I was able to get into a yellow cab and I couldn't ride a yellow cab in the south and the next impression was that the Negroes lived in such beautiful large homes homes like they were down on St. Charles Avenue and that was a great impression too and then as the years as I stayed there and time passed I found out that as I've often said that the Negroes were doing things I saw Negro lawyers where I didn't see Negro lawyers in the south and they had many different chances for opportunities there only thing to give a Negro at my time and I was a girl an inspiration was to be a nurse or a school teacher but in Chicago there were many professions that was the opportunity for Negroes to grasp and they did yes now when you first went there and started to sing did you get paid for your singing no not at all well I got four hours one night you spend all that money how were you able to support yourself well I was working on the north side around Sheridan Road doing laundry work over there and I was doing factory work and that's how I was able to support myself and how were you finally discovered well I was singing at a funeral on the south side and in the early days way back when it was the OK record company and Decca was this man called the talent he was a talent scout and he heard me sing at this funeral and offered me this opportunity to come and ask me did I want to make records well that was the greatest thing that had ever been said to me you know especially to sing religious songs yes he's the one that took the chance on the Decca label yeah for religious songs
